To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The model-based performance test can be applied to a variety of sensors, eco-zones, and class definitions; 2) The MD classifier is more sensitive to intra-class variation than the ML and FB classifiers; 3) The avocado plantation was the only class that was confounded with a forest type for all classifiers; 4) Oak forest was the most distinguishable forest type, and the secondary tropical and pine forests were the least distinguishable forest types.

the minimum distance (and the maximum likelihood) classification is more sensitive to differences in forest types than the frequency-based one, and that the avocado plantation is confounded with the tropical forest.
the minimum distance classifier, with a 25 m spatial window, is the most appropriate for the NFI map, and that the avocado plantation is confounded with primary tropical forest.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantification of ambiguities in the context of accuracy assessment and with the identification of the sources of these ambiguities.
the quantification and understanding of the ambiguities that affect the accuracy of forest maps derived from remotely sensed imagery.

the development and application of a model-based performance test to forest classifiers on remote sensing images, with the goal of identifying and quantifying the ambiguities between forest types, in the sense of three common classifiers (MD, ML, and FB).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ambiguity of the NFI classification is not due to the sensor type (IKONOS) nor to the classification method (ML), but rather to the forest class definitions used in the NFI.
the MD classifier is the most sensitive to ambiguity, followed by the ML classifier, whereas the FB classifier is less sensitive to ambiguity.
the MD classifier is the most appropriate for mapping forest communities, but that the ML classifier is the most suitable for mapping forest types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ambiguity pattern of forest types in the NFI of Mexico is consistent with the confusion matrix of the accuracy assessment.
the ambiguity between classes is not a simple function of their structural or spectral differences, but also depends on the type of classifier used.
, in order to improve the accuracy of forest inventories, the use of remote-sensing data must be complemented by the use of ancillary data (e.g., leaf optical properties) and a model-based analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ambiguity of forest classes on imagery is a function of the classification rule and the window size.
the choice of classifier and the window size are critical in the interpretation of the results of the confusion matrix.
a systematic analysis of the ambiguity between forest classes is a prerequisite for the design of forest inventories and for their interpretation.
